questions.stem: Which is a condensed structural formula for butane?
questions.explanation: A condensed structural formula shows each carbon with its attached hydrogens in order along the chain. C₄H₁₀ is the molecular formula, which gives only the number of each atom, and C₂H₅ is the empirical formula.

questions.stem: A skeletal structure shows a zigzag line with six carbon positions and a double line between the second and third positions from one end. What is the compound?
questions.explanation: In a skeletal structure each end and vertex is a carbon atom, so there are six carbons, and the double line is a C=C bond. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives it position 2, so the name is hex-2-ene.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbons (butane), with a methyl group on each of carbons 2 and 3. Two identical groups are shown by the prefix di- and both locants. A methyl on carbon 1 would simply lengthen the chain.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain containing the double bond has four carbons. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond places it at carbon 1 and the methyl group on carbon 2. Naming it as a propene with an ethyl group misses the longest chain.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The main chain has five carbons and includes the triple bond. Numbering must give the triple bond the lowest locant, so it is between carbons 2 and 3 and the methyl group is on carbon 4. Numbering to favour the methyl group gives the wrong name 2-methylpent-3-yne.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain runs through the ethyl group and has six carbons, with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4 when numbered to give the lowest locants. Naming it as a pentane with an ethyl group fails to find the longest chain.

questions.stem: Counting hexane itself, how many chain isomers have the molecular formula C₆H₁₄?
questions.explanation: They are hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane. Other drawings, such as a methyl group on carbon 1 or an ethyl group on carbon 2, are one of these molecules redrawn.

questions.stem: Which C₆H₁₄ isomer has the lowest boiling point?
questions.explanation: All the isomers have the same number of electrons, but the more branched and compact a molecule is, the less surface contact it has with its neighbours and the weaker its dispersion forces. 2,2-dimethylbutane is the most compact, so it boils lowest, and straight-chain hexane boils highest.

questions.stem: What is the general formula of the alkynes with one triple bond?
questions.explanation: Each triple bond in place of a single bond removes four hydrogen atoms from the alkane formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, giving CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. CₙH₂ₙ is the general formula of the alkenes.

questions.stem: Why do the alkanes, alkenes and alkynes belong to different homologous series?
options: Alkenes and alkynes contain oxygen, while alkanes contain only C and H
Each has a different type of carbon-carbon bond and general formula
Each contains a different element bonded to the carbon chain
Each series has a different number of carbon atoms per molecule
questions.explanation: A homologous series shares one general formula and functional group, so its members have similar chemical properties. The C-C single bonds of alkanes, the C=C of alkenes and the C≡C of alkynes give each series its own formula and reactivity. All three are hydrocarbons.

questions.stem: What is the shape around each carbon atom of a carbon-carbon triple bond?
options: Linear, with a bond angle of 180°
Bent, with an angle of about 105°
questions.explanation: Each triple-bonded carbon has two regions of electron density, which are as far apart as possible in a straight line. Double-bonded carbons are trigonal planar and single-bonded carbons are tetrahedral.

questions.stem: Which alkene has geometric (cis and trans) isomers?
questions.explanation: Geometric isomers need two different groups on each carbon of the C=C bond. In but-2-ene each carbon has an H and a CH₃. But-1-ene, propene and 2-methylpropene each have one double-bond carbon carrying two identical groups.

questions.stem: Why do geometric isomers of alkenes exist?
options: Rotation about the C=C double bond is restricted
The C=C double bond rotates freely at room temperature
Alkenes contain carbon atoms with only three bonds
The two isomers have different molecular formulas
questions.explanation: The double bond prevents rotation, so groups fixed on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans) cannot interconvert. Each carbon still forms four bonds, and the isomers share a molecular formula.

questions.stem: Including geometric isomers, how many alkene isomers have the molecular formula C₄H₈?
questions.explanation: They are but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene. Forgetting that but-2-ene has two geometric isomers gives 3.

questions.stem: Which pair of compounds are position isomers?
questions.explanation: Position isomers have the same carbon chain and functional group but differ in its position, here the triple bond. The cis and trans pair are geometric isomers, butane and 2-methylpropane are chain isomers, and but-1-ene and butane have different formulas.

questions.stem: Why does but-2-yne, CH₃C≡CCH₃, have no geometric isomers, while but-2-ene does?
options: But-2-yne has two identical methyl groups, which cancels the isomerism
The C-C≡C-C unit is linear, so each triple-bond carbon has only one other group
The triple bond rotates freely, so the cis and trans forms convert rapidly
But-2-yne has fewer carbon atoms than but-2-ene, so it has fewer isomers
questions.explanation: Each carbon of a triple bond forms just one other bond, and the four carbons lie in a straight line, so there is no 'same side' or 'opposite side'. But-2-ene's trigonal planar carbons each carry two groups, allowing cis and trans forms. Both compounds have four carbons.

questions.stem: What is the main hazard when handling gaseous hydrocarbons such as propane and butane in the laboratory?
options: They are highly flammable and can form explosive mixtures with air
They are strongly acidic and corrode skin on contact
They are radioactive and must be stored behind shielding
They react violently with water to release toxic gases
questions.explanation: Propane and butane ignite easily, and leaking gas can form an explosive mixture with air; they are also denser than air, so they collect in low places. Naked flames must be kept away and the area well ventilated.

questions.stem: How should waste liquid hydrocarbons, such as hexane, be disposed of in a school laboratory?
options: Poured down the sink with plenty of water
Evaporated over a Bunsen burner flame
Mixed with acid and placed in the bin
In a labelled organic waste container
questions.explanation: Liquid hydrocarbons are flammable, insoluble in water and harmful to waterways, so they must not go down the sink. They are collected in a labelled organic waste container for proper disposal; heating them near a flame risks fire.

questions.stem: Hexane and hex-1-ene are each shaken with bromine water in the dark. What is observed?
options: Neither has any reaction, because bromine needs a catalyst
Hex-1-ene decolourises the bromine water quickly; hexane does not
Hexane decolourises the bromine water quickly; hex-1-ene does not
Both decolourise the bromine water quickly at the same rate
questions.explanation: The C=C bond in hex-1-ene undergoes a fast addition reaction with bromine, removing the orange-brown colour. Hexane has only single bonds and reacts by substitution only slowly, and only in ultraviolet light.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular forces act between molecules of pentane?
questions.explanation: Pentane is a non-polar hydrocarbon, so the only attractions between its molecules are dispersion forces from temporary dipoles. It has no O-H, N-H or F-H bonds for hydrogen bonding, and no permanent dipole.

questions.stem: Chloroethane boils at 12 °C, while ethane boils at −89 °C. What best explains the difference?
options: The polar C-Cl bond adds dipole-dipole forces, and Cl adds electrons for dispersion
Chloroethane forms hydrogen bonds through its chlorine atom and its hydrogen atoms
Chloroethane has stronger covalent bonds that must break when the liquid boils
Ethane is an ionic compound whose ions separate easily when it is heated
questions.explanation: The C-Cl bond makes chloroethane polar, so dipole-dipole forces act between its molecules, and the chlorine atom also increases the number of electrons, strengthening dispersion forces. Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, and H bonded to carbon does not hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂, is a polar molecule, but tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is non-polar. Why?
options: The C-Cl bonds in CCl₄ are non-polar, but in CH₂Cl₂ they are polar
CCl₄ has a trigonal planar shape, so its bond dipoles add together
CH₂Cl₂ contains hydrogen bonds, which make the whole molecule polar
In CCl₄ the four C-Cl dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel
questions.explanation: Both molecules are tetrahedral and both contain polar C-Cl bonds. In CCl₄ the four identical dipoles point symmetrically and cancel, while in CH₂Cl₂ the different C-H and C-Cl bonds do not cancel, leaving a net dipole.

questions.stem: Which straight-chain alkanes are gases at 25 °C and 100 kPa?
questions.explanation: Methane (−162 °C), ethane (−89 °C), propane (−42 °C) and butane (close to 0 °C) all boil below room temperature. Pentane boils at 36 °C, so the alkanes from pentane to octane are liquids at 25 °C.

questions.stem: Why do the boiling points of the straight-chain alkanes rise from C1 to C8?
options: Longer molecules have more hydrogen bonds between them, so more energy is needed
Longer molecules have stronger C-C covalent bonds, which must break when boiling
Longer molecules are more polar, so their dipole-dipole forces are stronger
Longer molecules have more electrons and contact, so dispersion forces are stronger
questions.explanation: Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and surface area, so the temporary dipoles are larger and the dispersion forces between molecules stronger. Alkanes remain non-polar, have no hydrogen bonds, and keep their covalent bonds intact when they boil.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₂Cl?
questions.explanation: Numbering from the chlorine end gives the lower set of locants, 1 and 2, rather than 2 and 3. Substituents are listed in alphabetical order, so bromo comes before chloro: 2-bromo-1-chloropropane.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCl?
questions.explanation: The central carbon carries three methyl groups and a chlorine. The longest chain is three carbons, with both the chlorine and a methyl group on carbon 2. Naming it as an ethane misses the longest chain.

questions.stem: What is the product when ethene reacts with hydrogen chloride?
questions.explanation: In an addition reaction the H and Cl of HCl add across the double bond, giving CH₃CH₂Cl. Adding Cl₂ would give 1,2-dichloroethane, and chloroethene still contains a double bond.

questions.stem: Propene reacts with hydrogen chloride. Which products can form?
questions.explanation: Propene is unsymmetrical, so the Cl can add to either carbon of the double bond, giving a mixture of 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane (mainly 2-chloropropane). Addition consumes the whole HCl molecule, so no hydrogen gas is released.

questions.stem: But-2-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide. How many different haloalkane products can form?
options: One, 1-bromobutane, because Br adds to the end carbon
One, 2-bromobutane, because the alkene is symmetrical
questions.explanation: Both carbons of the double bond in CH₃CH=CHCH₃ are equivalent, so adding Br to either one gives the same product, 2-bromobutane. Two products form only when the alkene is unsymmetrical, as with propene or but-1-ene.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the reaction of propene with bromine?
questions.explanation: Bromine adds across the double bond, one Br on each of the two double-bonded carbons, giving 1,2-dibromopropane. Replacing an H and releasing HBr would be substitution, and the Br atoms do not end up on carbons 1 and 3.

questions.stem: Hex-1-ene is mixed with hydrogen gas over a platinum catalyst. What type of reaction occurs and what is the product?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen adds across the C=C bond in the presence of a metal catalyst such as platinum or nickel, converting the alkene into the saturated alkane hexane. Nothing is replaced, so it is not substitution, and the product has fewer multiple bonds, not more.

questions.stem: Methane and chlorine react in ultraviolet light to form chloromethane. What are the reaction type and the other product?
questions.explanation: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. A chlorine atom replaces a hydrogen atom, which leaves combined with the other chlorine atom as HCl. Alkanes have no double bond, so they cannot undergo addition.

questions.stem: When methane reacts with excess chlorine in ultraviolet light, the product contains CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄ as well as CH₃Cl. Why?
options: Methane decomposes in the light, and its carbon then reacts with chlorine
The hydrogen chloride formed reacts with methane to add more chlorine
The hydrogens of chloromethane can be substituted in turn by more chlorine
Chlorine adds across the C-H bonds of methane, one bond at a time
questions.explanation: Chloromethane still has C-H bonds, so it can undergo further substitution, giving dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane. This is why substitution of alkanes gives a mixture of products that must be separated.

questions.stem: Alkenes react with bromine at room temperature, but alkanes react only in ultraviolet light. Why?
options: The C=C double bond is stronger than a single bond, so it attracts bromine
Alkanes contain fewer hydrogen atoms, so there are fewer sites for bromine
The C=C double bond is reactive, while alkanes have only strong C-C and C-H bonds
Alkanes are polar, so they repel the bromine molecules unless light is present
questions.explanation: Part of the double bond breaks easily, so bromine can add across it without extra energy. Alkanes have only strong single bonds, so they need ultraviolet light to start substitution. A double bond is stronger than one single bond but weaker than two, and alkanes have more hydrogens than alkenes, not fewer.

questions.stem: Methane is used mainly as a fuel. Which properties suit it to this use?
options: It is a solid that releases energy slowly as it dissolves in water
It is a gas that is easily piped and burns releasing much energy
It is a liquid that is easily stored and burns with a sooty flame
It is a reactive gas whose double bond lets it polymerise readily
questions.explanation: Methane, the main component of natural gas, has a very low boiling point, so it is a gas that can be piped to homes and industry, and its combustion is highly exothermic with a clean blue flame when air is sufficient. It has no double bond.

questions.stem: Why is ethene, rather than ethane, the starting material for making polyethylene and many other chemicals?
options: It has a higher boiling point, so it is a liquid
It burns more cleanly, so it is safer to store
It is non-flammable, so it is safe to process
Its double bond undergoes addition reactions readily
questions.explanation: The reactive C=C bond lets ethene undergo addition polymerisation and addition reactions to make ethanol, chloroethane and other products. Ethene is a flammable gas at room temperature, like ethane.

questions.stem: Propane burns completely: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. What mass of CO₂ (M = 44.01 g mol⁻¹) forms when 2.20 g of propane (M = 44.09 g mol⁻¹) burns?
questions.explanation: n(C₃H₈) = 2.20 / 44.09 = 0.0499 mol, and each mole gives 3 mol of CO₂, so n(CO₂) = 0.150 mol and m = 0.150 × 44.01 = 6.59 g. Assuming a 1 : 1 ratio gives about 2.20 g.

questions.stem: 5.61 g of ethene (M = 28.05 g mol⁻¹) reacts completely with excess bromine. What mass of 1,2-dibromoethane (M = 187.9 g mol⁻¹) forms?
questions.explanation: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ is 1 : 1. n(C₂H₄) = 5.61 / 28.05 = 0.200 mol, so m = 0.200 × 187.9 = 37.6 g. The value 32.0 g is the mass of bromine that reacts, not of the product.
